intro_en:
A desert segment of the Israel National Trail with gentle walking and a few surprises: a large sand dune that looks as if it arrived from the seashore, and unusual archaeological sites.

 Nahal Tzihor - Shizafon Junction (49)
 Shaharut - Be'er Milhan (51)
character_en: Easy walking for most of the way, with a few short climbs
transport_en: At the start point: Shizafon base and Shizafon Junction. At the end point: the community of Shaharut (low frequency)
pois_en: Neot Smadar (a community near the trail). The Nahal Kasuy dune. The Uvda Valley. The Leopards Temple. Khan Shaharut (north of the community)
important_en: At the foot of the Nahal Kasuy dune there are overnight campsites (no water).
The segment ends north of the community of Shaharut. There is a khan there that offers lodging, water refills and basic food supplies.

The trail does not pass by the community of Shaharut itself. You can sleep and stock up on drinking water at the segment's end point at Khan Shaharut. Food supplies can be obtained via a Shufersal Online delivery, which reaches the community of Shaharut several times a week.
description_en:
The Israel National Trail leaves Shizafon Junction heading south-west on a dirt track parallel to Road 12 and north of it. Road 12 leaves Shizafon Junction southwards, passes through the Uvda Valley and continues parallel to the border with Egypt as far as Eilat.
At Nahal Hiyyon, the Israel National Trail leaves the shoulder of Road 12. We turn south under the bridge and walk along the edge of the stream channel, parallel to a high-voltage power line. On the other side of the channel is the entrance road to the community of Shaharut.
After a stretch of walking, the trail approaches the entrance road to Shaharut and crosses it eastwards at the point where Nahal Kasuy passes under the road through a low bridge.
The Israel National Trail climbs gently onto a ridge. At the high point at the top of the ridge, the dunes of the Kasuy Sands are suddenly revealed. The sand spilled like this on the eastern side of the ridge is the result of environmental conditions and the composition of the rocks and soil in the immediate area. A combination of weathering whose product is sand and a suitable wind regime carries the sand to this point and creates this special scenery.
To the west lies the Uvda Valley - named after an operation conducted at the end of the War of Independence, in early 1949. In parallel with the armistice talks between Israel and Egypt and Jordan, Operation Uvda was carried out, the last operation of the War of Independence, whose aim was to establish facts (uvdot) on the ground by capturing the southern Negev and the Eilat area. The Negev and Golani Brigades moved south in a pincer movement through the Negev and the Arava to Umm Rashrash at the head of the Gulf of Eilat. The Arabic name of the Uvda Valley is Wadi al-Uqfi, meaning the beam of a threshing sledge - a tool used for threshing grain on the threshing floor. The name may testify to the valley's agricultural character.
In 1979 a comprehensive archaeological survey was conducted in the Uvda Valley, ahead of the evacuation of the IDF airfields in Sinai as part of the peace treaty with Egypt and the construction of a new military airfield in the Uvda Valley. The survey and salvage excavations uncovered hundreds of sites in the valley and its surroundings from various periods, from the Neolithic period to the later periods. Among the finds: remains of dwellings, temples, water reservoirs and threshing floors. All of these show that the Uvda Valley was home to extensive human life and activity throughout history.
From the top of the dune you can proceed in two ways. One is to continue with the trail marking along the edge of the plateau and descend to the road. The second, recommended way is to go down the dune running, rolling or jumping. After the descent, we continue on a red-marked dirt track that heads south from the foot of the dune to the entrance road to Shaharut.
When the Israel National Trail returns to the road, we continue south beside the road, walking along the edge of the Uvda Valley.
After a short while we reach the main archaeological site of the Uvda Valley, known as the "Leopards Temple". The site lies at the foot of hills standing east of the road, and is surrounded by a low iron fence.
On the western side of the compound there is a rectangle enclosed by stones. It is thought to be the courtyard of a temple with a small room at its western corner - the cult room or "holy of holies". The temple apparently functioned in the mid-6th millennium BCE, in the Neolithic period. Beside the temple an artistic depiction was uncovered, made of small limestone slabs set upright in the ground. The depiction shows 15 animals with tails curled upwards, facing east. It is assumed that the animals represent leopards. One animal with long horns faces the opposite direction and may represent an antelope. The animal depiction has been partly damaged, and one can distinguish between the original parts and those that were reconstructed. The reconstructed parts are made of small stones with larger gaps between them.
We continue south and reach several more archaeological sites that the Israel National Trail passes through or beside. This is a small sample of the hundreds of sites surveyed in the Uvda Valley, most of which are not freely accessible because they lie within the grounds of the military airfield. Among other things, we pass a dwelling from the Nabataean period and the remains of structures and compounds from earlier periods.
The abundance of sites in the Uvda Valley, an area that today receives only about 30 mm of rain a year on average, may come as a surprise. But it turns out that thousands of years ago there was settlement here and even agricultural activity such as growing wheat. According to researchers' estimates, about 3,000 settlers lived in the valley in the third millennium BCE, a period when the climate in the region was far wetter.
The Israel National Trail turns left heading east and climbs a low hill. We walk a stretch along the back of a narrow spur between Nahal Re'uel and Nahal Shaharut. The trail descends from the spur heading south, and climbs gently up the tributaries of Nahal Shaharut.
While crossing a low spur, you can make out a built circle and beside it a row of stones set upright in the ground - further ancient remains of a cult installation.
The Israel National Trail descends to a broad plain and reaches the entrance road to Shaharut, the end point of the segment.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
